name: Light Grape Green
lede: Light Grape Green is a muted, greyish yellow-green named for the grape, plotted by Ridgway in 1912 and classed by the ISCC-NBS system in 1955 as a moderate yellow green.

sections.title: A grape, not a grape color
sections.body:
Our data traces the name to the grape rather than to a pigment or a place [1]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas plots it on plate XLI at hue 25‴, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files the same area as block 120, "moderate yellow green," about 5.7 units from that block's reference point [1]. In LCH terms it reads as lightness 67, chroma 22, hue 110 degrees: soft, low in saturation, and closer to olive than to true green [1].

Its nearest neighbors by computed color distance are almost indistinguishable: [[oyster-grey|Oyster Grey]] and [[eucalyptus|Eucalyptus]], each only 3.0 units off, and [[artichoke-green|Artichoke Green]], 3.4 units off [2]. The closest everyday name is Sage, about 5.9 units away [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a close match covers enough of the canvas in 901, as photographed (511 by the stricter within-painting measure), which makes it more common than 83 percent of the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in paintings from the 1900s, at 1.9 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive (63 of 1,674 paintings) [4]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 40 percent of its matches, by lightness rank within the canvas; varnish cannot fake that ranking [4].

[[painter:niels-larsen-stevns|Niels Larsen Stevns]] used it most: it appears in 5 of his 22 works here, 5.9 times the rate of the museums those works come from, 5.8 times as photographed [4]. The earliest match is a painting from 916, nearly a thousand years before the name's first record in 1912; that only shows the hue existed long before anyone wrote it down, not that any pigment did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. On canvas it keeps company with [[glass-green|Glass Green]] and [[kronberg-s-green|Kronberg's Green]] more often than chance [4].
